r-p6-01:0.why: L yes: A (both elevators out of service until March 20) follows 'five days' and 'therefore' smoothly in its own place. D yes: the next paragraph opens 'The elevator that remains in service', singular, which only C supplies and A contradicts. B yes: A is the most natural continuation of 'the work will take five days'. S no. Low end of hard, because the contradiction sits in the very next sentence. B is dead on the dates already given in the first sentence and subject line; D contradicts paragraph 3 (the loading dock stays in use).

r-p6-01:1.why: L no: 'them' parses with the nearest plural noun 'the stairs', but 'use the stairs ... and leave them free' contradicts itself; 'one' has no noun to point to inside the sentence; 'theirs' fits nowhere. D yes (antecedent 'the elevator' is in the previous sentence) and B is arguably yes (nearest-noun pull), but with no distractor that reads sensibly in its own sentence the item is easy by 8.3.
r-p6-01:1.fix: Not wrong. If a harder pronoun item is wanted, give 'them' a sensible nearby plural antecedent, or replace this blank with a vocabulary or connective blank. Only one item in this set is easy, which is within the 10% limit.
r-p6-01:1.editorNote: 'leave one free' is the only other form that is grammatical with an elevator reading, but the previous sentence says only one elevator remains in service, so 'one' (an unspecified member of several) conflicts with the document. Not flagged.

r-p6-01:2.why: L yes: 'even if' reads smoothly in the sentence alone ('postponed even if they come early in the morning'). D yes: paragraph 3 (freight elevator open to tenants for these deliveries 6-8 a.m.) rules it out and confirms 'unless'. B no, S no: 'unless' is also the natural exception word, so most readers settle it inside the sentence. 'because' and 'although' are illogical.

r-p6-01:3.why: L yes: 'has been' and 'was' are grammatical in the sentence alone. D yes: the clue is the March 9 date and paragraph 1 ('will begin' on March 16), not this sentence. B no: nobody confidently believes present perfect here. S no: the whole e-mail is future-oriented, so it is one step. 'had been' has no past reference point.
r-p6-01:3.editorNote: 'has been open ... each weekday' could be misread as a standing arrangement already in force, but 'these deliveries' are the postponed ones and the work has not started, so an editor would change it to 'will be'. No in-sentence cue exists; the item relies on the header date plus paragraph 1. Not flagged.

r-p6-02:0.why: L yes: 'Nevertheless' is grammatical and sensible in a lone sentence; 'As a result' too. D yes: the previous sentence (far fewer rejected claims) decides, and 'Nevertheless' would need a negative result. B no, S no: only two options survive locally, and the previous sentence is clearly positive. 'Otherwise' and 'For example' fail even alone. Lower edge of medium.

r-p6-02:1.why: L yes: 'no longer need to keep the original receipts' reads smoothly in its own sentence. D yes: the next sentence ('Our auditors may ask to see the originals') is what kills it and supports 'still'. B yes: the previous sentence ('receipts are simply photographed') makes 'no longer' the expected word. S no. 'not yet' and 'already' are not sensible even locally.
r-p6-02:1.editorNote: 'no longer' is excluded only by the single sentence after the blank (keeping originals for six months, then auditors asking to see them). That is a clean exclusion, not an assumption, so it is not ambiguous.

r-p6-02:2.why: L yes: C (claims after that date are no longer accepted) follows a deadline sentence naturally. D yes: the next sentence ('Claims submitted late will be repaid the following month instead') only works if on-time claims are repaid in the same month (A) and contradicts C ('no longer accepted' versus 'repaid'). B yes: C is the most expected follow-up to a deadline. S yes: the blank 4 sentence has to be read to see 'instead'. B ('later date') is wrong because the 5th is earlier than the 15th; D contradicts the October 1 replacement of paper forms.

r-p6-02:3.why: L yes: 'lately' parses ('claims submitted recently'). D yes: the deadline sentences and 'instead' show the sense 'after the deadline'. B no: late/lately is a familiar pair, so a good student does not confidently choose 'lately'. S no. 'lateness' and 'latter' are not adverbs.
r-p6-02:3.editorNote: 'lately' is the only rival; it means 'recently', so 'Claims submitted lately' does not carry the missed-deadline meaning that 'instead' requires. An editor would change it. Not flagged.

r-p6-03:0.why: L yes: A reads naturally after 'the ovens run around the clock' (a new site, so the old one closes). D yes: A is excluded only by paragraph 3 ('Mill Road will be left to concentrate on bread', 'will continue to bake some pastries'); C is excluded by 'Until now, everything ... at its original bakery'; D by 'run around the clock'. B yes: A is the assumption most readers bring. S no. B is confirmed by the next sentence (narrow lot between a school and houses).

r-p6-03:1.why: L yes: 'will begin' and 'has begun' are both grammatical and sensible in the sentence alone. D yes: the dateline (June 12) is at the top of the article, far from the blank. B yes: 'will begin' fits an announcement article, and 'has begun' fits work in progress. S yes: compare the dateline with 'in March', conclude March is past, then reject present perfect with a finished-time adverbial. 'had begun' has no past reference point.
r-p6-03:1.editorNote: 'has begun in March' is the near miss. Present perfect with a finished-time adverbial ('in March') is not standard formal English in either variety, so it is a legitimate trap, but the item leans on that one rule. Not flagged.

r-p6-03:2.why: L yes: 'Once' is grammatical and sensible in its own sentence. D yes: the previous sentence ('Mill Road will be left to concentrate on bread') plus 'continue' and the October opening show the pastries are a temporary carry-over, so 'Until'. B yes: 'Once' is the believed rival. S no. 'Even though' asserts that the new site is already at full capacity (it has not opened); 'In case' makes no sense.
r-p6-03:2.fix: Tighten so that 'Once' cannot be read as a permanent exception, for example change 'will be left to concentrate on bread' to 'will eventually bake only bread'.
r-p6-03:2.editorNote: Near miss: 'Once the new site is running at full capacity, however, Mill Road will continue to bake some pastries' can be read as a permanent carve-out, because 'concentrate on bread' does not strictly say 'only bread'. It sits badly with the stated reason ('room for all of Corvell's pastry production') and with 'continue', so it needs an extra assumption. Not ambiguous, but a careful editor could query it.

r-p6-03:3.why: L yes: 'obligation', 'instruction' and 'necessity to transfer' are grammatical and plausible in the sentence alone. D yes: the previous sentence ('no current employee will be required to move') excludes all three. B no: 'be given the opportunity to' is the dominant collocation, and none of the rivals is something a good student believes. S no.

r-p6-04:0.why: L yes: 'Like the printed magazine, the digital edition will reach you on the first' reads smoothly alone. D yes: paragraph 2 says the printed copy arrives a week or more after the first. B no: the late print copy is the point of the letter. S no. 'Despite' and 'Except for' are illogical.
r-p6-04:0.editorNote: 'Like' is excluded because it would say the printed copy reaches readers on the first, which paragraph 2 denies. Clean exclusion. Not flagged.

r-p6-04:1.why: L yes: A (those who already renewed keep the old rate) reads as a natural follow-up to a price cut. D yes: the next sentence says subscribers who already paid 'will receive a refund of the difference', which contradicts A and requires C. B yes: A is the expected business practice, so readers believe it. S no. B contradicts 'fall'; D contradicts the $30 print surcharge ($72 + $30 is not $96) and does not link to the refund sentence.

r-p6-04:2.why: L yes: 'whom' reads smoothly in the window ('Subscribers whom our records show'). D yes: the deciding word is 'have already paid', after the inserted 'our records show'. B yes: 'whom' is the over-correction good students believe. S yes: strip the insertion to see that the relative pronoun is the subject of 'have paid'. 'whose' and 'which' fail.
r-p6-04:2.editorNote: 'whom' is an over-correction (4.2), not a defensible second answer. Good trap.

r-p6-04:3.why: L yes: 'Would you prefer to keep receiving the magazine by mail' is a complete, natural question in the window. D yes: the comma and 'please check' are about ten words after the blank. B no: the 'Should you ..., please' pattern is well known in business letters. S no. 'Were you prefer' and 'Had you prefer' are ungrammatical.
r-p6-04:3.editorNote: Careful that 'Were' stays a wrong answer: 'Were you to prefer' would be correct, but 'Were you prefer' is not. As written it is fine.

shouldFix: r-p6-03:2 - option A 'Once' is a near miss (can be read as a permanent exception that Mill Road keeps some pastries after the new site is running at full capacity). Tighten with 'will eventually bake only bread' (or equivalent) so that only 'Until' works.
overall: No ambiguous items: for all 16 questions the keyed answer is the only one that is correct standard formal English and coherent with the whole document. Band count: hard 8 (r-p6-01:0, r-p6-02:1, r-p6-02:2, r-p6-03:0, r-p6-03:1, r-p6-03:2, r-p6-04:1, r-p6-04:2), medium 7, easy 1 (r-p6-01:1, pronoun with no locally sensible rival). That is 50% hard and 6% easy, which meets the round 7 target (hard >= 50%, easy <= 10%) only just; r-p6-01:0 is the weakest 'hard'. Each document has exactly one sentence insertion and three word blanks, no more than one item per document is easy, answer letters are balanced (A5 B4 C3 D4), and no keyed answer appears as a distractor in another item. Compared with the official Part 6 format (8.0): same document types and E-mail/Memo/Letter headers, four blanks, one insertion; word counts (135-185 without the insertion sentence) are a little longer than the sample, and the blanks lean on a distant clue more than the sample's mostly local ones, so the set is harder than the sample. Best items: r-p6-02:1 (still / no longer), r-p6-02:2 and r-p6-04:1 (insertions killed by the next sentence), r-p6-03:1 (dateline tense). Weakest: r-p6-01:1 (easy pronoun), r-p6-02:0 (single-step connective). Batch topics are all announcements of an operational change with a deadline, and the 'however / instead' discourse pattern recurs in three documents; consider one different genre next round. Consistency checks: March 16 is a Monday and March 16-20 is five days, which matches 'five days'; $96 to $72 plus a $30 print option is consistent with the refund of the difference; all dates (Mar 9 / Sep 2 / Jun 12 / Sep 15) agree with the tenses keyed. All names look invented; 'Southmere' is a common-sounding place name and carries a very small risk of matching a real one.
